Paragraph:
Translation: It is better to live in this world by begging than to live at the cost of the lives of great souls who are my teachers. Even though they are avaricious, they are nonetheless superiors. If they are killed, our spoils will be tainted with blood.

Purport: According to scriptural codes, a teacher who engages in an abominable action and has lost his sense of discrimination is fit to be abandoned. Bhisma and Drona were obliged to take the side of Duryodhana because of his financial assistance... But Arjuna thinks that nevertheless they remain his superiors, and therefore to enjoy material profits after killing them would mean to enjoy spoils tainted with blood.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna declares his absolute preference for a life of poverty and humiliation (begging) over achieving victory through the death of his revered elders.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: He acknowledges the flaws of his elders ('avaricious'), but maintains that their status makes killing them unforgivable. He concludes that any victory won this way would be 'tainted with blood.'
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna entrenches himself in his refusal, proposing to abandon his royal duties entirely and become a mendicant.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.escapism: Fleeing reality, Choosing humiliation over responsibility
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.black and White Thinking: Seeing no middle ground between sin and poverty

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Sannyasa (Renunciation, which Arjuna is attempting to adopt falsely to escape duty)
Bhiksa (Begging, the livelihood of a renunciate)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The purport clarifies a key spiritual rule: a teacher who loses their discrimination and sides with evil should be abandoned. Arjuna, blinded by material sentiment, fails to apply this higher principle. He proposes a false renunciation (living by begging) to avoid the painful but necessary execution of justice.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Arjuna is demonstrating severe escapism driven by anticipatory guilt. To avoid the trauma of killing his teachers, he romanticizes a life of begging. He views the situation in black-and-white terms: either he commits an unforgivable sin and lives with 'blood-tainted' spoils, or he gives up his entire life to beg. He sees no healthy resolution.
